page.title: Inverted index
page.text: An inverted index is the data structure that makes keyword search possible. Instead of storing, for each document, the list of words it contains, it stores for each word the list of documents that contain it. That inversion is the whole trick: answering which documents contain a term becomes a single dictionary lookup rather than a scan of the entire collection. Most inverted indexes also record the positions at which each term occurs, which costs memory and buys the ability to answer phrase queries.

page.title: Forward index
page.text: A forward index maps each document to the list of terms it contains. It is the natural way to store a collection and the wrong way to search one, because answering a query requires visiting every document. Forward indexes are still built during index construction, as an intermediate step before inversion, and they are useful for tasks such as generating snippets where you need a document's own contents.

page.title: Tokenization
page.text: Tokenization splits a stream of text into the units that will be indexed. The simplest rule keeps maximal runs of letters and digits and discards everything else, which handles English reasonably and fails on languages that do not put spaces between words. Decisions made here set a ceiling on everything downstream: a token the tokenizer never produces is a token no amount of clever ranking can retrieve. Case folding usually happens here too, so that a query for Apple matches a document that says apple.

page.title: Stemming
page.text: Stemming reduces inflected words to a common form so that a query for connecting finds a document that says connect. It is a crude process that works by stripping suffixes according to rules rather than by understanding the language, so it sometimes conflates words that are unrelated and sometimes fails to conflate words that clearly belong together. The Porter stemmer is the best known algorithm for English. Stemming increases recall and can reduce precision, and it is not reversible: you cannot recover the original word from its stem.

page.title: Lemmatization
page.text: Lemmatization maps a word to its dictionary form using a vocabulary and a morphological analysis of the word. Unlike stemming, which chops suffixes mechanically, lemmatization knows that better is a form of good and that ran is a form of run. It is more accurate and considerably more expensive, and it needs a language resource that stemming does not.

page.title: The Porter stemming algorithm
page.text: The Porter stemmer applies five phases of suffix stripping rules to an English word. Each rule fires only when the stem left behind has enough syllable structure, measured by a quantity the algorithm calls m, which counts alternations between vowel and consonant sequences. This measure is what stops the rules from destroying short words. The algorithm is deterministic, fast, and famously produces stems that are not real words: relational becomes relate, and rational stays rational.

page.title: Stopwords
page.text: Stopwords are words so common that knowing a document contains one tells you almost nothing. The, of, and, is, to. Removing them shrinks the index where it is fattest, because their postings lists are the longest in the collection. The cost is that some queries genuinely need them: to be or not to be consists entirely of stopwords. Modern systems tend to keep stopwords and let the ranking function give them almost no weight, which achieves the same effect without losing the ability to match them.

page.title: Term frequency
page.text: Term frequency counts how often a term occurs in a document. The intuition is that a document mentioning a word ten times is more about that word than one mentioning it once. Raw counts are rarely used directly, because the relationship is not linear: the tenth occurrence tells you much less than the second did. Logarithmic damping and saturating functions are the two usual corrections.

page.title: Inverse document frequency
page.text: Inverse document frequency measures how much knowing that a document contains a term actually tells you. A term appearing in every document separates nothing and is worth nothing; a term appearing in three documents out of a million is enormously informative. The usual formula is the logarithm of the number of documents divided by the number containing the term. It is the reason a search for the red car ranks on car rather than on the.

page.title: TF-IDF weighting
page.text: TF-IDF multiplies term frequency by inverse document frequency, so a term counts for a lot when it appears often in this document and rarely in the collection as a whole. It is the classical weighting scheme for the vector space model and remains a reasonable baseline. Its main weakness is that term frequency enters linearly and without limit, so a document that repeats a word twenty times scores twenty times a document that mentions it once, which does not match how relevance actually behaves.

page.title: The vector space model
page.text: The vector space model represents each document and each query as a vector over the vocabulary, with one dimension per distinct term. Relevance becomes a geometric question: how close is the query vector to the document vector. Because documents are short relative to the vocabulary, these vectors are overwhelmingly zero, and any practical implementation stores only the non-zero components. The model discards word order entirely, which is the bag of words assumption.

page.title: Cosine similarity
page.text: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors rather than the distance between their tips. This matters for retrieval because a long document has a longer vector simply by virtue of being long, and distance would reward that. Dividing each vector by its own length removes the effect, and once both vectors have unit length the cosine is just their dot product. It is the standard similarity measure for the vector space model.

page.title: Document length normalization
page.text: Long documents contain more terms and therefore match more queries, which gives them an unearned advantage that has to be corrected. Cosine normalization divides by the vector length. Pivoted length normalization adjusts that correction because pure cosine over-penalizes long documents relative to how often users actually judge them relevant. BM25 takes a third approach, comparing each document's length against the collection average and letting a parameter control how much that comparison matters.

page.title: BM25
page.text: BM25 is a probabilistic ranking function that has been the strongest simple baseline in information retrieval for three decades. It differs from TF-IDF in two ways that matter. Term frequency saturates, so the tenth occurrence of a word adds far less than the second did, controlled by a parameter conventionally between 1.2 and 2.0. And document length enters explicitly, comparing each document against the collection average, with a second parameter conventionally set to 0.75 controlling how strong that effect is. It is called BM25 because it was the twenty-fifth best match formula tried in the Okapi project.

page.title: Probabilistic retrieval
page.text: Probabilistic retrieval models rank documents by their estimated probability of being relevant to the query. The probability ranking principle states that ranking by this probability is optimal under a stated set of assumptions. The binary independence model is the simplest such model, and BM25 is the best known function to come out of this line of work.

page.title: Boolean retrieval
page.text: Boolean retrieval answers whether a document matches a query expressed with and, or and not. It returns a set rather than a ranking, which is its strength for expert users who want exact control and its weakness for everyone else, because a query returning ten thousand documents in no particular order is not useful. Legal and medical search still use Boolean queries heavily, because being able to state exactly what you want is worth more there than convenience.

page.title: Phrase queries
page.text: A phrase query requires terms to appear adjacent and in the stated order, which is what distinguishes a search for the phrase computer science from a search for documents containing both words anywhere. Answering one requires positional information in the index. The standard technique subtracts each term's offset within the query from its positions in the document, so that every term of a genuine occurrence maps onto the same number and adjacency becomes a set intersection.

page.title: Positional index
page.text: A positional index stores, for each term and each document containing it, the list of positions at which the term occurs. This roughly doubles or triples index size compared to storing document identifiers alone, and it is what makes phrase queries and proximity ranking possible. Positions within a document are strictly increasing, which is exactly the property that makes them compress extremely well when stored as gaps.

page.title: Proximity ranking
page.text: Proximity ranking boosts documents in which the query terms appear close to one another, on the reasoning that words near each other are more likely to be about the same thing than words at opposite ends of a long document. It sits between bag of words scoring, which ignores order entirely, and phrase matching, which demands exact adjacency. Most production ranking functions include some proximity component.

page.title: Postings list
page.text: A postings list is the list of documents associated with one term in an inverted index, together with whatever per-document information the index keeps: term frequency, positions, field markers. Postings lists follow a very skewed distribution, with a handful of terms accounting for most of the total size. Query processing is largely the business of intersecting and merging these lists efficiently.

page.title: Skip pointers
page.text: Skip pointers let an intersection jump forward in a postings list rather than walking every entry. They pay off when one list is much longer than the other, because the walk over the long list can then skip most of it. They cost space and they complicate the format, and they help nothing when the lists are of similar length, so whether to add them is a question to settle with a measurement rather than an argument.

page.title: Variable byte encoding
page.text: Variable byte encoding stores an integer in as few bytes as possible, using seven bits of each byte for data and the top bit as a continuation flag. Numbers below one hundred and twenty eight take a single byte. It is simple, fast to decode, and byte aligned, which makes it much easier to work with than bit level schemes even though those achieve better compression ratios.

page.title: Delta encoding
page.text: Delta encoding, also called gap encoding, stores the differences between consecutive values rather than the values themselves. Because document identifiers in a postings list are sorted, and positions within a document are sorted, the gaps are small numbers even when the original values are large. This is what makes variable byte encoding worth applying: small numbers compress and large ones do not.

page.title: Index compression
page.text: Index compression reduces the size of an inverted index, which matters for two reasons that are usually stated in the wrong order. It saves disk space, which is cheap. More importantly it saves time, because a compressed index means fewer bytes read from disk, and decompression is fast enough that the trade is almost always worth it. The standard combination is to delta encode the sorted values and then variable byte encode the resulting small gaps.

page.title: Index construction
page.text: Index construction turns a collection of documents into an inverted index. The naive approach accumulates everything in memory and fails as soon as the collection exceeds available memory. Blocked sort based indexing writes sorted blocks to disk and merges them. Single pass in memory indexing builds complete dictionaries per block, avoiding the need to hold a global term to identifier mapping. Both are essentially external sorting problems in disguise.

page.title: Index segments
page.text: Rather than maintaining one index that must be rebuilt whenever a document changes, most modern search engines write many small immutable segments and merge them in the background. Immutability buys a great deal: readers never need locks, a query can run while indexing continues, publication of new data is atomic, and recovery after a crash amounts to ignoring any segment the manifest does not name. Deletions become tombstones, because you cannot remove a posting from an immutable file.

page.title: Log structured merge trees
page.text: A log structured merge tree buffers writes in memory, flushes them as immutable sorted runs, and merges those runs in the background into progressively larger ones. It trades read amplification for write amplification, which is the right trade when writes are frequent and reads can afford to consult several runs. The design underlies many storage engines and is the same idea search engines use for index segments.

page.title: Memory mapped files
page.text: Memory mapping presents a file as a region of memory and lets the operating system fetch pages on demand. For a search index this means the whole file never has to be loaded: a query touches a few postings lists and only those pages are read. The technique works best when access is sparse and random, which describes query processing exactly, and it hands page replacement to a kernel that is already good at it.

page.title: Term dictionary
page.text: The term dictionary maps each term in the vocabulary to the location of its postings. For an in-memory index a hash table is the obvious choice. For an on-disk index the dictionary needs to support lookup without reading the whole thing, which a sorted array with binary search achieves simply, and which a finite state transducer achieves in far less space while also supporting prefix queries.

page.title: WAND query processing
page.text: WAND is a document at a time query evaluation strategy that avoids scoring documents which cannot possibly enter the top results. It keeps an upper bound on each term's maximum contribution and uses those bounds to skip forward past documents whose best possible score falls below the current threshold. Block max WAND refines this by storing maxima for blocks of postings, so entire blocks can be skipped rather than individual documents.

page.title: Top k retrieval
page.text: Users look at ten results, so computing exact scores for a million matching documents is almost entirely wasted work. Top k retrieval returns only the best k, and the algorithms that do it well stop early rather than scoring everything and sorting. A heap of size k is the simple version, turning an n log n sort into n log k. Early termination strategies go further and avoid even looking at most candidates.

page.title: Precision and recall
page.text: Precision is the fraction of returned documents that are relevant. Recall is the fraction of relevant documents that were returned. They trade against each other: returning everything gives perfect recall and useless precision, and returning one certain hit gives the reverse. Which one matters more depends entirely on the task. A patent search cares about recall because missing prior art is expensive; a web search cares about precision because nobody looks past the first page.

page.title: Mean average precision
page.text: Average precision recomputes precision at the rank of each relevant document and averages the results, which rewards ranking relevant documents higher rather than merely including them somewhere. Mean average precision averages that across a set of queries, and it is the standard single number for comparing two retrieval systems because it accounts for both what came back and the order it came back in.

page.title: Discounted cumulative gain
page.text: Discounted cumulative gain evaluates a ranking using graded relevance judgements rather than a binary relevant or not. Each result contributes its grade discounted by the logarithm of its rank, so a highly relevant document at position one is worth much more than the same document at position ten. Normalizing by the score of the ideal ranking gives a number between zero and one that is comparable across queries with different numbers of relevant documents.

page.title: Relevance judgements
page.text: A relevance judgement records that a human considered a particular document relevant to a particular query. They cannot be derived from the collection, they are expensive to produce, and every offline evaluation depends on them. The critical discipline is that judgements must be made before the results are seen, because a judgement made afterwards follows the system it is meant to be judging and the comparison becomes worthless.

page.title: Test collections
page.text: A test collection is a corpus, a set of queries, and relevance judgements for them. Cranfield established the methodology in the nineteen sixties and TREC has run it at scale since nineteen ninety two. The point is repeatability: two systems evaluated on the same collection with the same measure can be compared, and a change can be shown to help rather than merely claimed to.

page.title: Query expansion
page.text: Query expansion adds terms to a query in the hope of matching documents that use different words for the same idea. Synonyms are the obvious source. Relevance feedback derives the extra terms from documents the user marked relevant, and pseudo relevance feedback simply assumes the top few results were relevant and expands from those, which helps on average and fails badly when the top results were wrong.

page.title: Spelling correction
page.text: Spelling correction matters more in search than in most applications, because a misspelled query returns nothing at all rather than something slightly wrong. The usual approach measures edit distance between the query term and terms in the dictionary, restricted to candidates that share enough character n-grams to be worth checking. Correction can be applied silently or offered as a suggestion, and which is right depends on how confident the correction is.

page.title: Edit distance
page.text: Edit distance counts the minimum number of insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to turn one string into another. The standard algorithm fills a matrix and runs in time proportional to the product of the two lengths. For spelling correction the full matrix is usually unnecessary, because you only care whether the distance is below a small threshold, which allows the computation to be cut off early.

page.title: Snippets
page.text: A snippet is the short extract shown under each result, and it is what lets a user decide whether to click without opening the page. Generating one requires the original document text, which an inverted index does not keep, so a separate document store is needed. The usual approach scores candidate passages by how many query terms they contain and how close together those terms are, then highlights the matches.

page.title: Web crawling
page.text: A crawler fetches pages, extracts their links, and fetches those in turn. Doing it politely means respecting robots exclusion rules and not overwhelming any single host, which turns a simple graph traversal into a scheduling problem. Duplicate detection matters enormously, because a large fraction of the web is near duplicate content, and a crawler that does not notice will spend most of its budget re-fetching the same text.

page.title: Distributed search
page.text: Splitting a collection across machines is usually done by document, giving each machine a complete index of its own slice. A query goes to every shard, each returns its local best results, and a coordinator merges them. The subtlety that catches people is that inverse document frequency is a collection-wide statistic, so computed per shard the same term gets different weights on different machines and the scores are no longer comparable.

page.title: Caching in search engines
page.text: Search engines cache at several levels: parsed queries, the postings lists of popular terms, and complete result pages. Query traffic is extremely skewed, so a small cache catches a large fraction of requests. Invalidation is the hard part, and immutable index segments help enormously, because a cache entry keyed by segment can never become stale.

page.title: Hash tables
page.text: A hash table maps keys to values in constant expected time by computing a numeric hash of the key and using it as an index into an array. Collisions are unavoidable and are handled either by chaining entries in a list or by probing for another free slot. Performance degrades as the table fills, so implementations resize when the load factor crosses a threshold.

page.title: B-trees
page.text: A B-tree keeps sorted data in a shallow, high fanout tree so that a lookup touches few nodes, which matters when each node is a disk block. It is the structure underneath most relational database indexes. Compared with a log structured merge tree it favours reads and in-place updates over write throughput.

page.title: Binary search
page.text: Binary search finds a value in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the range under consideration, taking logarithmic time. It is trivial to describe and famously easy to get wrong, with off by one errors at the boundaries and overflow in the midpoint calculation being the two classic mistakes.

page.title: Unicode normalization
page.text: The same visible text can be represented by different sequences of code points. An accented letter may be a single composed character or a base letter followed by a combining mark, and the two look identical while comparing as unequal. Normalization forms C and D compose and decompose respectively. The compatibility forms KC and KD go further, folding ligatures and full width characters, which is usually what a search engine wants and is not reversible.

page.title: Regular expressions and backtracking
page.text: A regular expression engine that backtracks can take exponential time on inputs constructed to make it do so, which turns a pattern in a query path into a denial of service vector. Patterns with nested quantifiers and alternation are the dangerous shapes. A single character class with one quantifier cannot backtrack at all and is linear on every input.

page.title: Growing tomatoes
page.text: Tomatoes need full sun, a deep soil that drains well, and consistent watering, since irregular watering is what causes the fruit to split. Pinch out side shoots on cordon varieties to keep the plant putting its energy into fruit rather than foliage. Feed weekly once the first truss has set, and pick them when they come away from the stem with a gentle twist.

page.title: Making filter coffee
page.text: Grind the beans to the coarseness of sea salt just before brewing, because ground coffee goes stale within minutes. Use around sixty grams of coffee per litre of water, off the boil rather than boiling, and pour in slow circles so that all the grounds are wetted evenly. The whole brew should take about four minutes.

page.title: Query processing
page.text: Query processing is everything that happens between a user pressing enter and results appearing. The query text is analyzed with exactly the same pipeline used when indexing, because a query analyzed differently asks for terms the index never stored, and the engine then returns nothing while appearing to work perfectly. The analyzed terms are looked up in the term dictionary, which yields a postings list for each. Those lists are then combined: intersected for a conjunctive query, merged for a disjunctive one, and checked for adjacency when the query is a phrase. The result is a set of candidate documents, and candidates are not yet an answer. Each candidate is scored by the ranking function, and only the best few are kept, which is why implementations use a heap of size k rather than sorting everything. There are two broad strategies for the scoring loop. Term at a time processing walks one postings list to completion, accumulating partial scores in a table of document identifiers, then moves to the next term. It is simple and it needs an accumulator per candidate document, which is memory proportional to the number of matches. Document at a time processing advances all the postings lists together, in document order, and completes each document's score before moving on. It needs far less memory and it is what makes early termination possible, because once a document's score is final you can compare it against the current threshold and decide whether anything further is worth examining. Modern engines use document at a time processing for exactly that reason. The final step is presentation: fetching titles, generating snippets from the stored document text, and highlighting the terms that matched. That step needs the original text, which the inverted index does not keep, so a separate document store is required.

page.title: The text analysis pipeline
page.text: Everything a search engine can ever retrieve is decided by the analysis pipeline, because a term it does not produce is a term no query can find. The pipeline runs in a fixed order and each stage constrains the ones after it. First the text is decoded and normalized. Unicode allows the same visible string to be written as different sequences of code points, so an accented character may be one composed code point or a base letter followed by a combining mark; without normalization the two forms never match each other even though they render identically. Next comes tokenization, splitting the stream into indexable units. A rule that keeps maximal runs of letters and digits works acceptably for English and produces nothing at all for Chinese, Japanese and Korean, which do not separate words with spaces and need either dictionary based segmentation or character n-grams. Case folding usually happens here, so that a query for Apple finds a document that says apple, at the cost of no longer distinguishing the company from the fruit. Then common words may be removed. This shrinks the index where it is fattest, because the postings lists of the most frequent words are by far the longest, but it makes some queries impossible to express. Finally the surviving tokens are reduced to a common form by stemming or lemmatization, so that inflections of the same word meet on one term. The critical rule is that this exact pipeline must be applied to queries as well as documents. If the two paths ever diverge, the failure is silent: no error is raised, no test necessarily fails, and the engine simply returns nothing for queries that should have matched.

page.title: Ranking signals
page.text: A modern ranking function combines many signals rather than relying on one. The textual signals come first. Term frequency measures how often a query term occurs in the document, damped or saturated so that repetition stops helping after a point. Inverse document frequency weights each term by how rare it is across the collection, so a match on an unusual word counts for far more than a match on a common one. Document length is used to stop long documents winning simply by containing more words. BM25 combines these three and remains the strongest simple baseline in the field. Beyond the bag of words there are structural signals. A term matching in a title is worth more than the same term in the body, which BM25F handles by weighting each field separately before combining them, rather than by scoring the fields independently and adding the results. Proximity signals reward documents in which the query terms appear near one another, on the reasoning that words close together are more likely to be about the same thing. Phrase matches are the extreme case of the same idea. Then there are signals that have nothing to do with the text at all: how many other documents link to this one, how recently it was published, how often users click it when it appears, and how quickly they come back to search again afterwards, which is a strong negative signal. Once click data exists, a learned model over all of these features beats any hand tuned combination, which is what learning to rank means. The important discipline is that every added signal must be justified by a measured improvement on held out judgements, because signals interact and adding one that helps in isolation can easily make the whole worse.

page.title: Keeping an index up to date
page.text: An index built once and never changed is a much simpler thing than an index that has to track a changing collection, and almost every real system needs the second. The naive approach rebuilds everything whenever anything changes, which is correct, simple, and impossible once a rebuild takes hours. The approach that actually works writes small immutable segments. New documents accumulate in an in-memory buffer; when it fills, the buffer is written out as a segment file that is never modified again. A query consults every segment and merges the results. Because segments are immutable, readers need no locks, a query can run safely while indexing continues, and a crash leaves at worst a half written file that recovery can ignore. Publication is made atomic by writing a manifest naming the segments that count, so a segment exists only once the manifest mentions it. Deletion cannot work by removing a posting, since the file is immutable. Instead a per segment set of deleted document identifiers is kept, results are filtered against it at query time, and the space is actually reclaimed only when segments are merged. This is why deleting from a production search system does not immediately free disk. Updating a document is a delete followed by an insert. Segment count grows without bound unless something merges them, and merging is the background process that combines several small segments into one larger one. A merge policy decides which segments to combine and when, trading query cost, which rises with segment count, against write cost, which rises with merging. Tiered policies merge segments of similar size, which is the same idea as a log structured merge tree. A change to the analysis pipeline is the hard case, because old and new documents are then analyzed differently and queries match neither correctly. The standard answer is to record the analyzer version in the index and rebuild into a new index when it changes, swapping an alias once the new one is verified.

page.title: Compression of postings
page.text: An uncompressed inverted index is several times the size of the text it was built from, which is why compression is not an optimization in this field so much as a requirement. The reason it pays is not disk space, which is cheap, but time: fewer bytes read from disk means less waiting, and modern decompression is fast enough that the decoding cost is much smaller than the input and output cost it saves. The techniques rely on making the numbers small before trying to store them in fewer bits. Document identifiers within a postings list are sorted, and positions within a document are sorted, so storing the differences between consecutive values rather than the values themselves turns large numbers into small ones. This is delta or gap encoding, and it is always the first step. Once the numbers are small, a variable length code stores each one in as few bytes or bits as it needs. Variable byte encoding uses seven bits of each byte for data and the eighth as a continuation flag, so a number below one hundred and twenty eight occupies a single byte. It is byte aligned, which makes it simple and fast to decode. Bit level codes such as Elias gamma and Golomb achieve better ratios by not wasting the padding that byte alignment implies, at the cost of much slower decoding, and the trade has generally moved in favour of the faster byte aligned schemes as processors got faster relative to memory. Frame of reference and its patched variants encode a block of values relative to a common base, which vectorizes well on modern hardware. The term dictionary compresses too, usually by front coding, which stores each term as the length of the prefix it shares with the previous term plus the remaining suffix, exploiting the fact that a sorted vocabulary has long shared prefixes.

page.title: Evaluation methodology
page.text: Deciding whether one retrieval system is better than another is harder than it sounds, and the discipline for doing it was established by the Cranfield experiments in the nineteen sixties and industrialized by TREC from nineteen ninety two. The apparatus has three parts: a document collection, a set of queries, and relevance judgements saying which documents answer which query. The judgements are the expensive part and the part everything else depends on. The cardinal rule is that judgements are made before the systems are compared. A judgement made after seeing what a system returned is contaminated, because the judge is now reacting to the output rather than assessing the document, and a comparison built on contaminated judgements can confirm anything. For the same reason the queries must be chosen before the results are seen, or the query set quietly becomes a description of what the system already does well. Metrics divide into set based and rank based. Precision and recall treat the results as a set and ignore order entirely. Average precision recomputes precision at the rank of every relevant document and averages, which rewards putting good results near the top, and mean average precision extends that across a query set to give one comparable number. Discounted cumulative gain uses graded rather than binary judgements and discounts each result by the logarithm of its rank, then normalizes against the ideal ordering so that queries with different numbers of relevant documents can be averaged together. No offline measure captures everything. Judgements decay as collections and user expectations change, small differences are frequently not statistically significant, and pooling means the judged set is biased toward what earlier systems retrieved. Production systems therefore supplement offline evaluation with online experiments, interleaving two rankings or running an A B test, while keeping a fixed regression set so that a change cannot quietly make things worse.

page.title: String dictionaries
page.text: Every search engine needs to map a term to information about it, and the structure chosen for that mapping has consequences well beyond lookup speed. A hash table gives constant expected time and is the obvious choice while the dictionary lives in memory. It cannot answer anything about the neighbourhood of a key, so prefix and range queries are impossible, and it must be held in memory in its entirety. A sorted array with binary search costs a logarithm instead of a constant but supports range and prefix queries naturally, and it can live on disk: only the blocks a binary search touches need to be read, so the dictionary never has to be fully loaded. Storing every term in full wastes space when a sorted vocabulary shares long prefixes between neighbours, which front coding removes by recording the shared prefix length and the differing suffix. A trie stores terms by their characters, so a lookup follows one edge per character and a prefix query is simply the subtree below a node. The cost is a large number of small nodes and poor memory locality. A finite state transducer is a trie whose common suffixes have also been merged, giving a directed acyclic graph that maps each term to a value while storing shared structure once. It is dramatically smaller than a trie or a plain sorted array, supports prefix and wildcard queries, and is what a modern search library uses for its term dictionary. The price is that it is complex to build and immutable once built, which is acceptable precisely because index segments are immutable anyway.

page.title: Scaling a search service
page.text: A single machine holds a search index until it does not, and the order in which things break is predictable enough to plan around. Memory goes first, because a positional index is several times the size of the source text. Compression and moving postings to disk both attack that, and memory mapping the index file lets the operating system page in only what queries actually touch. Build time goes next, and the fix is parallelism: analysis is the dominant cost and documents are independent, so it parallelizes almost perfectly across processes. When one machine can no longer hold the collection at all, it is split across several. Sharding by document gives each machine a complete index of its own slice; a query is broadcast to every shard, each returns its own best results, and a coordinator merges them into a final ranking. This scales collection size and query throughput at the same time and is what nearly everyone does. It has one trap that catches people repeatedly: inverse document frequency is a statistic over the whole collection, so if each shard computes it locally the same term is weighted differently on different machines and the scores coming back cannot be meaningfully merged. Either accept the approximation, which is usually tolerable when documents are assigned to shards randomly, or distribute global term statistics periodically. The alternative, sharding by term so that each machine owns part of the vocabulary, is better for single term queries and much worse for everything else, because multi term queries then require postings to cross the network before they can be intersected. Replication is added for availability and read throughput, and it brings a distributed systems problem with it: leader election, stale replicas, and rebalancing when a machine joins or fails. Caching helps enormously because query traffic is extremely skewed, and immutable segments make cache invalidation tractable since an entry keyed by a segment can never go stale.

page.title: Recall
page.text: The fraction of all relevant documents that a search actually returned. A system that returns everything has perfect recall.

page.title: Precision
page.text: The fraction of returned documents that are relevant. High precision means little rubbish in the results.

page.title: Corpus
page.text: The collection of documents a search engine indexes and searches over. Also called the collection.

page.title: Vocabulary
page.text: The set of distinct terms appearing anywhere in the corpus. Its size determines how many dimensions a document vector has.

page.title: Document frequency
page.text: The number of documents in the corpus that contain a given term. Not to be confused with term frequency, which counts occurrences within one document.

page.title: Query
page.text: What the user types. The engine analyzes it with the same pipeline used for documents, then matches and ranks.

page.title: Relevance
page.text: Whether a document actually answers the user's need. It is a judgement made by a person and cannot be computed from the collection.

page.title: Token
page.text: One unit of text produced by the tokenizer, before stopword removal and stemming turn it into an indexed term.

page.title: Term
page.text: An entry in the index, produced by analyzing a token. A term is often not a real word, because stemming truncates.

page.title: Ranking
page.text: Ordering matched documents by how well they answer the query. Matching decides which documents qualify; ranking decides which come first.

page.title: Search engine
page.text: A system that builds an index over a corpus and answers queries against it with a ranked list of documents.

page.title: The BM25 parameters
page.text: Two parameters control BM25. The first, k1, sets how quickly term frequency saturates, conventionally between 1.2 and 2.0. The second, b, sets how strongly document length is corrected for, conventionally 0.75, where zero disables length normalization entirely and one applies it fully.
